newsitem.title: GREECE: Defiant Greek farmers camp out by road barricades.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Greek farmers camp out by road barricades.

text.p: A stretch of Greece's national highway looks more like a squatter camp, with farmers huddled under makeshift tents strung between tractors or handing out bread and feta cheese to "comrades".
Loudspeakers hung amid the sea of tractors crank out defiant old communist party songs -- although the protesters come from all across the political spectrum, they like the defiant tone.
Farmers guard chained entrances on either side of the camp blocking a length of the highway near this central farm town.
Scores of similiar camps have sprung up across Greece since farmers began blocking roads and railways 11 days ago to press economic demands in a showdown with the socialist government.
The protests have frozen transport around Greece, traffic across the Bulgarian and Turkish borders has ceased and Greek markets are running out of produce as Christmas approaches.
"People from villages all across the country have come to the blockades with food, firewood, whatever they can give," said a farmer who has a tractor parked among thousands.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis has rejected demands for higher price supports, cheaper fuel prices and rescheduling of debts. He says everyone must make sacrifices if Greece wants to be an equal player in European Union.

"Why is it that there is never enough to go around when it comes to farmers?" asked a man sitting by a fire of tyres and tree branches. "I don't know much about the budget, but these demands are not new, we've been asking for them for years."

Farmers say that as long as it doesn't rain too often they will be happy to sit it out, playing cards and backgammon. They have brought tables and chairs into their tents along with photographs and Christmas trees to make them more cozy.

The walls of their "homes" are the sides of tractors. Some with generators have hooked up lights and television sets. But bits of white road lining on a tent floor reminds the farmers they are in the middle of the national highway.

"No one really wants to be here, we would rather be in our warm homes or drinking a coffee at the local cafeteria," said Andonis Theodoropoulos, a cotton producer. "But I have a family at home I can't afford to feed."
The smell of burning rubber and smoked meat is ever present. Whole fresh lambs are roasted on spits over the fires.
The wives and children join the farmers at night, and the wine and ouzo flow while now and then someone pulls out a guitar or bouzouki and farmers dance around the tractors.
"We want them back home, where they can have a proper meal," said one farmer's wife. "We don't want to spend Christmas like this." The farmer's children are playing on the tractors.
Vaios Sakas, 24, said he wants to continue producing cotton like his father, but worries about his future.
"I don't want these problems when I have a family, it's not worth it." he said.
On either side of the blockades an empty highway stretches for miles. Three km (miles) away, dozens of lorries are trapped by the blockades, sitting under a thick fog that has covered the region.
Local and foreign drivers impatiently wait for the blockade to end.
"We were held up by the truckers strike in France, then in Italy, now here," Philip Judge from Oxford who was delivering meat to Azerbaijan said. "We are going to miss Christmas with our children."
They sleep in their cabs at night. Food and water are scarce and a hot shower too far away by foot. Drivers from Turkey, Bulgaria, Denmark, Germany and England are equally frustrated.
"I understand the farmers' problems, I sympathise, but what has that got to do with us?" said one driver.

They have staged their own protest, lining their trucks along the road blocking farmers from moving between blockades. Every few days locals bring the lorry drivers sandwiches. Some sympathetic farmers deliver water, cheese and bread.
